chunks: First, how much it stores: high energy density, so watt-hours per kilogram and per litre, because that sets how big and heavy the battery has to be for a given runtime.
Second, how hard it can work: low internal resistance, so it can deliver high current without the voltage collapsing or the cell heating up.
Third, behaviour over time: long cycle life, low self-discharge, and ideally a flat voltage curve so the electronics see a steady supply.

Then the practical ones: safe, meaning it tolerates abuse and doesn't catch fire easily; wide temperature range, because capacity and resistance both get worse in the cold; fast charging; low cost; and the right form factor, like a thin pouch for a phone or a rugged cylinder for a tool.
You can't have everything, though. Chasing energy density tends to eat cycle life and safety margin. Chasing power means a thicker, lower-resistance cell with less energy.

So which ones are 'desirable' depends on the product: a drone wants specific power, an IoT sensor wants low self-discharge, a phone wants volumetric energy density, a power tool wants high current and robustness."
